title: Japan Weighs Nuclear-Powered Submarines and Lithuania Moves to Scrap Its Nuclear Ban as Asia's Naval Race and NATO's Eastern Flank Both Heat Up
subhead: Tokyo is considering putting nuclear-propelled submarines into its security documents for the first time, while Lithuania's parliament backs lifting its constitutional ban on nuclear weapons and offers to fund a permanent US base. Separately, Houthi strikes on Saudi airports killed three and Russia's deadliest night strike in weeks killed 28 in Ukraine.

sections.heading: Japan Signals a Break With Its Nuclear Taboo, and South Korea Follows
sections.body:
Japan's government is weighing whether to mention nuclear-powered submarines in the three national security documents it plans to revise by the end of the year — the first time Tokyo would formally open the door to a technology it has never fielded. Kyodo News, Jiji Press and the Yomiuri Shimbun reported that the plan under discussion would not commit Japan to acquiring such submarines, but would list them as an option worth studying, with officials arguing that long-range, long-endurance boats are increasingly necessary as China's navy extends its reach into the Pacific.

The move sits awkwardly against Japan's Atomic Energy Basic Law, which restricts nuclear power to peaceful uses and has been read for decades as barring military applications. The proposed language is deliberately soft — a research and debate hook rather than a procurement decision — but it is the clearest sign yet that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government is willing to test the boundaries of Japan's post-war constraints.

Tokyo is not alone. UPI reported that South Korea is also moving toward nuclear-powered submarines, with Seoul having secured US approval to pursue the capability alongside its new 3,000-ton indigenous boat. The two developments together mark a shift in Northeast Asia's naval balance that China and North Korea will read as a direct response to their own build-ups.
sections.whyItMatters: Nuclear-propelled submarines are a threshold capability: they require a nuclear propulsion program and signal a willingness to break with decades of restraint. If Japan and South Korea both move toward them, Northeast Asia's undersea balance shifts and China's ability to operate freely in the Pacific narrows.

sections.heading: Lithuania Votes to Remove Its Nuclear Ban and Offers to Pay for a US Base
sections.body:
Lithuania's parliament, the Seimas, backed the first reading of a constitutional amendment to remove the country's ban on nuclear weapons — a step toward potentially hosting allied nuclear arms. The vote, reported by LRT and the Kyiv Independent, follows President Trump's suggestion that he is considering a permanent US military base in Lithuania, and Lithuanian officials have said they would be willing to help fund it.

The Kremlin responded sharply. TASS reported that spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia would be forced to retaliate if nuclear weapons are deployed in Lithuania, calling NATO's military build-up near Russia's borders something Moscow 'cannot perceive' as anything but a threat. The disagreement is now a live test of how far NATO's eastern members can go in hosting nuclear infrastructure before Moscow escalates.
sections.whyItMatters: Nuclear sharing on NATO's eastern flank would harden the divide across the Baltic and give Russia a concrete grievance to act on, potentially through the hybrid tactics it already uses against the region. Lithuania is pushing the alliance's deterrence posture further east faster than the alliance has formally agreed.

sections.heading: Houthis Strike Two Saudi Airports, Killing Three, as Yemen's War Widens
sections.body:
Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports killed at least three people and injured 36, Saudi civil aviation authorities said. One of the targets was King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the kingdom's main gateway — a significant escalation in a conflict that had largely played out along Yemen's borders and the Red Sea. Al Jazeera, the Japan Times and Reuters all reported the strike, which prompted the Saudi-led coalition to strike back, saying it destroyed 82 Houthi military targets, including a missile platform used in the Riyadh attack.

On the ground, Yemen's internationally recognised government said its 'Dawn of Yemen' counter-offensive has 'neutralised' 1,860 Houthi fighters through 2,103 targeting operations. The claim, posted on social media and reported by Al Jazeera, could not be independently verified. Fighting has concentrated around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait — a route that has grown more important as the US-Iran conflict restricts traffic through Hormuz.
sections.whyItMatters: Hitting Riyadh's airport brings the war into the Saudi capital's core infrastructure and raises the risk that the conflict spreads to Gulf energy and aviation nodes. As Hormuz traffic is squeezed by the Iran war, Bab al-Mandeb becomes the next chokepoint to watch.

sections.heading: Russia's Deadliest Strike in Weeks Kills 28 Across Ukraine
sections.body:
Russian attacks across Ukraine on Wednesday killed at least 28 people, including five children, according to AFP and Reuters. In Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region, a missile hit a five-storey apartment block at about 6:30 am local time, killing 20 people, authorities said. Zelensky said three of the dead were 12-month-old infants and another was eight, and accused Moscow of deliberately targeting 'ordinary cities, ordinary life'. Interior ministry officials said another child's body was recovered from the rubble later in the day.

The strikes also targeted energy infrastructure, with reporting highlighting the risk of winter power losses and the strain on Ukraine's limited long-range air defence. The barrage came shortly after US envoys left Kyiv, where they had been pressing a revived push to end the war.
sections.whyItMatters: The scale and civilian toll — including infants killed in their sleep — will shape the diplomatic effort Washington is trying to restart. Strikes on energy ahead of winter are designed to make Ukrainian cities unlivable and pressure Kyiv at the negotiating table.

sections.heading: Oil Whipsaws Near $100 as G7 Unleashes Emergency Reserves
sections.body:
Oil markets swung sharply as the Houthi escalation and continued Iran-related uncertainty collided with a coordinated Western reserve release. Reuters reported that the IEA agreed to accelerate a release of oil stocks, with 100 million barrels still to come; the G7 agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude after what CNNBC described as a US export threat. France separately said it would release 10 million barrels of diesel from its stocks, per Reuters, and European nations moved to tap emergency fuel reserves.

Brent hovered around $100 a barrel while WTI traded near $88.50, with US stocks sliding as investors weighed supply-disruption risk against the reserve releases and fears of renewed major combat in the Iran war. US military planners have reportedly drawn up new options for a possible resumption of large-scale operations ahead of the midterm elections, according to NBC News.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is pricing a war premium that the reserve releases are only partly offsetting. With Bab al-Mandeb and Hormuz both under pressure, the buffer of emergency stocks is depleting faster than it is being refilled.

sections.heading: Rubio in Athens Urges a Nationalist West, and Brazil's Political Right Gains
sections.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio used a speech beneath the Acropolis in Athens to urge Western nations to reclaim what he called their civilisational roots, arguing that loyalty to one's own nation need not be selfish. The address, on the second leg of a NATO tour, blended reassurance about US support with the Trump administration's America-first doctrine, and framed stronger alliances and nationalism as complementary rather than opposed. India Today and other outlets reported the remarks.

In Brazil, thousands of student-led protesters marched after Flavio Bolsonaro topped the first round of the country's presidential election, DW reported. In Africa, the African Union launched the continent's first credit rating agency, aiming to offer an alternative to the major Western agencies, while Kenya carried out its first Ebola burial as contacts linked to its first confirmed case rose to 57, according to Anadolu Agency.
sections.whyItMatters: Rubio's framing is the clearest articulation yet of how Washington wants to reconcile alliances with nationalism — the message European partners will weigh as they debate defence spending and their own internal politics. Brazil's election and Africa's new ratings agency both signal a wider reshuffling of political and financial alignments outside the transatlantic core.

bottomLine: Today's clearest shift was nuclear: Japan moved to open debate on nuclear-powered submarines and Lithuania voted to scrap its nuclear weapons ban while offering to fund a US base, two separate tests of long-standing taboos that Russia and China will treat as provocations. In parallel, the Houthis struck Riyadh's international airport for the first time in this phase of the war and Russia killed 28 people in Ukraine in its deadliest night in weeks, while the G7 and IEA burned through emergency oil reserves to keep prices near $100. The common thread is that the fronts — Northeast Asia's naval race, NATO's eastern flank, the Gulf chokepoints and Ukraine's energy grid — are each hardening at the same time, with fewer and less effective buffers between them.
